attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. He links to news but makes the assertion himself.

semantics.note: 'Apparently' keeps the 'it seems'. The proposition leaves out 'by a single car' but keeps the two parts: aspirational, and not a single unedited run. Here 'it seems' signals second-hand reporting, and the sentence before it is firm ('Turns out Tesla staged'), so it is not a graded probability.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into capability and single-run parts is fair. Whether the speed-ups and camera cuts count as 'edited' is a question of reading; the contract fairly treats stitching runs together as the core of part two.

evidence.note: Reuters reports sworn testimony that the video showed what Tesla hoped to build, not what it could then do. Supports part one.
Pre-mapped route, driver takeovers in test runs, and a crash during the shoot. Supports the claim that the demo was staged and not real capability.
Primary deposition. Elluswamy says, as his understanding, that the final video was continuous and not stitched, though it took several attempts. Cuts against 'not a single run'.

Secondary, unsourced account that footage was edited to remove a barrier strike, and that the video has speed-ups and camera cuts. Conflicts with the sworn testimony, so it leaves the stitching question in dispute.

reviews.rationale: Part one holds: sworn testimony and Reuters reporting show the video was aspirational and did not reflect the car's real capability then. Part two, that it was not a single unedited run by one car, is contradicted by Elluswamy's sworn testimony that the final take was continuous and not stitched. Only a secondary account disputes that.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prose in his post. The embedded tweet is also his.

semantics.note: Faithful in substance. The proposition says 'AI-written', but the adjacent sentence says ChatGPT-written, and the contract rightly holds him to ChatGPT. 'First casualty' is rhetoric and is not scored.

contract.note: The plain reading (CNET published error-filled stories written with ChatGPT) is ordinary and fair, given that Marcus explicitly says 'ChatGPT-written stories'. A looser 'ChatGPT-style AI' reading would stretch the claim in his favour.

evidence.note: Independent report: 41 of 77 AI-written stories were corrected. Supports 'a lot of' mistakes.
CNET's own disclosure says the tool was an in-house engine, not ChatGPT. This is a company statement, not an independent finding, but nothing in the packet rebuts it.

reviews.rationale: The error part holds: an independent report shows more than half of CNET's 77 AI stories needed corrections. The ChatGPT part is contradicted by CNET's statement that it used an in-house engine, not ChatGPT. That statement is a company disclosure, but it is unrebutted. 'First casualty' is not scored.
